title: Seven Months After a Brain Stimulation Session Made Him Laugh, the Urge Returned Within Five Minutes
text:
Seven Months After a Brain Stimulation Session Made Him Laugh, the Urge Returned Within Five Minutes
The first time, the laughter came in bursts of up to 40 seconds while a magnetic coil pulsed over his head. The second time, seven months later, it did not even get that far. Within about five minutes of restarting the same brain stimulation treatment, the 48-year-old stroke patient felt a strong urge to laugh, and his doctors shut the machine off.
That return visit is one of the most telling details in a case series published Sept. 4 in Frontiers in Psychiatry. Neurologists Shusheng Jiao and Xiuhong Xu of Bethune International Peace Hospital in Shijiazhuang, China, describe two men who began laughing involuntarily during repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, or rTMS, used to help their arms recover after stroke.
The authors argue that the episodes were seizure-like events, and that the second encounter suggests the vulnerability did not simply fade.
A Routine Rehab Protocol with an Unexpected Side Effect
Both men had ischemic strokes on the right side of the brain. To help with weakness in the arm, they received low-frequency, 1 Hz rTMS over the hand area of the left motor cortex, a standard approach meant to calm the healthy hemisphere so the injured one can recover. Each daily session lasted 20 minutes and delivered 1,032 magnetic pulses at 70% of each man's resting motor threshold.
The 48-year-old began laughing during his third session. The episodes lasted 5 to 40 seconds. He told his doctors the laughter was "completely involuntary" and "not funny at all," and that he felt embarrassed and confused.
The second patient, a 42-year-old man, felt an urge to laugh in his fourth session and laughed during his fifth, for 5 to 30 seconds at a time. He told them that "even though it looked like laughing, it didn't feel like laughing at all."Afterward, he felt restless and uneasy, a pattern the authors describe as post-ictal dysphoria.
In both men, moving the coil to the left prefrontal cortex stopped the laughter, and putting it back over the motor cortex brought it back. Treatment was stopped, and both made a near-complete recovery. The younger man was back at work with no measurable disability at three months.
The Rechallenge That Changes the Picture
The older patient returned in February 2025 with new weakness on his left side, and the team tried the same protocol again. This time the urge to laugh arrived within roughly five minutes. Stimulation was stopped, and no full laughing episode followed.
The authors read that as evidence that susceptibility persists. In their safety discussion, they recommend that clinicians actively ask patients about any urge to laugh, especially in the first week of treatment, and stop stimulation immediately and reassess the treatment plan if it appears.
They also argue the cases "challenge the assumption that low-frequency protocols are uniformly safe in the post-stroke population." Low-frequency rTMS is generally considered the gentler option, with a seizure rate the authors cite as under 0.1%. Acute and subacute stroke patients, they suggest, may form a higher-risk group because the brain around a fresh injury can be unusually excitable.
Why the Motor Cortex Might Set Off a Laugh
Laughter has its own brain circuitry, separate from the experience of finding something funny. In a famous 1998 report in Nature, Itzhak Fried and colleagues showed that electrical stimulation of the supplementary motor area, a region near the motor cortex, could make a patient laugh.
Jiao and Xu propose that stimulation over the motor cortex spread to nearby laughter-related regions, including the pre-supplementary motor area and parts of the anterior cingulate cortex, and that repeated sessions gradually lowered the threshold for setting them off. They describe the episodes as ictal laughter, consistent with gelastic, or laughter-type, seizures.
That label is their interpretation. Live EEG during stimulation was unusable because of electrical interference from the coil. A one-hour video EEG recorded right after one session showed scattered sharp waves that the authors call suggestive but "non-diagnostic." The second patient declined video and EEG recording entirely.
The episodes are also different from pseudobulbar affect, a condition that can follow stroke and causes sudden bouts of laughing or crying, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Here, the laughter was locked to the stimulation itself.
A Small Signal for a Growing Treatment
Stroke is common. The CDC reports that more than 795,000 people in the U.S. have one each year. Magnetic stimulation is used increasingly in rehabilitation research and already has FDA marketing authorization for conditions including major depression, migraine pain, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. The agency has said patients with a seizure history should discuss that with their provider before treatment.
The authors call it, to their knowledge, the first report of rTMS-induced ictal laughter in stroke patients, and they acknowledge major limits. There were only two patients and no comparison group. The coil was placed by hand rather than with a navigation system, and a pre-existing seizure tendency could not be ruled out.
The cases do not show that rTMS is unsafe for most people, and both men largely recovered. Patients who notice any unusual urge, movement, or sensation during brain stimulation should tell the treating team right away.
Key Questions Answered
What happened when the patient was re-treated?
Seven months after his first episodes, the same protocol produced a strong urge to laugh within about five minutes. Doctors stopped stimulation before a full episode.
What is rTMS?
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation uses a magnetic coil held against the head to send pulses that change activity in targeted brain regions.
Were the laughing episodes seizures?
The authors believe so, but EEG during stimulation was unusable, and the readings afterward were not diagnostic.
Did the patients find anything funny?
No. One called it "not funny at all," and the other said it "didn't feel like laughing at all."
What do the authors recommend?
They advise clinicians to ask about any urge to laugh, especially in the first week, and to stop stimulation immediately and reassess the plan if it appears.
Is rTMS dangerous for stroke patients?
These two cases do not show that. Both men largely recovered, and the seizure rate the authors cite for low-frequency rTMS is under 0.1%.
